big: Dadi has built ₹1 crore and has stopped earning. She wants ₹50,000 a month from it. That is an SWP, and it depends on how the market behaves in the first few years.

lines: Can I take ₹50,000 every month from my ₹1 crore and still leave something for the grandchildren?
It may work. But the same withdrawals can end very differently in two markets. Let us watch both.

alt: Two lines showing what is left in the fund when withdrawals continue
caps: Both Dadis withdraw ₹50,000 a month, which is 6% of the corpus each year.
In the steady market the fund keeps growing while she withdraws.
In the market that falls early, the withdrawals bite into a smaller pile, and it never recovers.
The order of good and bad years matters. That is sequence risk.

title: A two-year buffer
stops: Sells no equity in a fall
Fixes a withdrawal rate too high
alt: A shield with a buffer's strengths and limits
caps: The answer is a buffer: two years of withdrawals in a steady fund.
In a fall, Dadi draws from the buffer and sells no equity at low prices.
It does not fix a rate that is too high, or promise the money lasts forever.

q: Dadi's ₹1 crore falls 25% in her first year, and she keeps withdrawing ₹6 lakh a year. Why does this hurt more than the same fall in year 15?
opts: An early fall shrinks the pile that all later withdrawals are paid from
Funds charge a higher expense ratio in the early years of a plan
Withdrawals made in year one are taxed more heavily than later ones
The market always recovers faster in the later years of any plan
why: Withdrawals take money out while prices are low, so fewer units are left to recover when the market turns. This is sequence risk.
Expense ratio is a yearly percentage of the fund's value. It does not depend on which year the withdrawal falls in.
Tax is on the gain portion of each withdrawal. It does not rise because the market fell in the first year.
No one can say later years recover faster. The point is that a fall hurts more when a withdrawal plan is already running.

q: Dadi redeems ₹1,00,000 from an equity fund. The units she sold had cost ₹60,000. How is the withdrawal taxed?
opts: Nothing is taxed because it is her own money
Only the ₹40,000 gain portion counts as capital gain
Only the ₹60,000 she originally invested is taxed
why: The part that was her own capital is returned to her. Taxing the whole amount would count that capital as profit.
Her capital comes back untaxed, but the gain on it does count. Tax rules apply to the profit in each withdrawal.
Each SWP payment is part cost and part gain. Only the gain is taxed, at the capital gains rate that applies to her holding period.
The ₹60,000 is her cost and is not taxed. Taxing it would charge her on money she already paid tax on.

q: Dadi asks for ₹50,000 a month from ₹1 crore. What is the sound reply?
opts: That is only 6% a year, so the money will certainly last as long as she lives
It is 6% a year and may work, but an early fall could drain it, so hold a buffer
Never withdraw more than ₹10,000 a month from any corpus, whatever its size
An SWP only works with a bank fixed deposit and not with a mutual fund
why: 'As long as she lives' is a promise nobody can keep. If returns come in below withdrawals, the corpus shrinks.
It names the rate, admits the risk of an early fall and gives a plan: a buffer and a yearly review.
There is no universal limit like this. The safe rate depends on the corpus, the mix of funds and the time she needs it.
An SWP is a feature of mutual funds. A bank fixed deposit has its own way of paying interest each month.

q: Why keep one to two years of withdrawals in a lower-risk fund?
opts: It raises the return earned by the equity part of the whole corpus
So she never has to sell equity after a fall to pay her monthly needs
It removes the tax that would otherwise apply to each withdrawal
It lets her withdraw more each month than the plan would allow
why: The buffer earns a low return. It supports the plan in a fall, it does not raise what equity earns.
In a falling market, bills are paid from the calm fund while equity has time to recover.
The tax on gains still applies to each redemption, whichever fund it comes from.
The buffer cannot raise a safe rate. A rate that is too high stays too high.

pts: An SWP redeems a fixed amount on a schedule. Only the gain part is taxed.
The order of good and bad years matters: an early fall plus withdrawals is the danger.
Keep one to two years of withdrawals in a steady fund.
